newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tycoon to be charged in January-prosecutor.
newsitem.headline: German tycoon to be charged in January-prosecutor.

text.p: German prosecutors said on Saturday they would file formal charges against disgraced property tycoon Juergen Schneider early next year, nearly three years after his empire collapsed under massive debts.
A spokesman for the Frankfurt public prosecutor's office told Reuters the charges against Schneider, who is being held in a local prison, would probably be submitted on January 3.

Schneider purchased some of Germany's most prestigious real estate in the post-unification property boom. He fled Germany in April 1994 with his wife Claudia, leaving behind a ruined business and five billion marks ($3.21 billion) in debts.

Schneider's lawyer Christoph Rueckel told the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily that Schneider would be formally charged with fraud and credit fraud as well as falsifying documents and fraudulent bankruptcy.
His wife would be charged with being an accessory to bankruptcy.
Two former associates, Mehdi Djawadi, alleged to have helped the Schneider plan their getaway, and Karl-Heinrich Kuepferle would also face charges, Rueckel told the paper.
Schneider and his wife were detained in Miami last year following a year-long international search. They returned voluntarily to Germany in February to face questioning.
Claudia Schneider has since been freed from prison on conditional release amid concerns about ill-health.

Frankfurt prosecutors said the trial was unlikely to begin before mid-1997. Rueckel said: "I anticipate the trial with great interest. It will be interesting to see if it will be possible to detail both the banks' and Schneider's role in obtaining loans."
Rueckel said that he planned to wait until the end of these proceedings to continue his efforts in demanding damages for Schneider from Deutsche Bank, once the tycoon's largest creditor.
Schneider has in the past denied the main thrust of the charges against him and accuses Deutsche Bank of ruining him.
Frankfurt prosecutors have said investigators had found no signs of wrongdoing on the part of Schneider's creditor banks and that there were no investigations against bank employees. ($1=1.5570 Mark)
